list.listitem: Suspect urethritis in sexually active men who present with dysuria, urethral pruritus and/or penile discharge. Gram stain of urethral secretions and urine testing can be used to confirm the diagnosis. C
All men with suspected or confirmed urethritis should be tested for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis using urine NAAT-based testing. C
Treat gonococcal infection with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose. Treat chlamydia with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. A
With persistent or recurrent urethritis, consider testing and treating for M. genitalium and T. vaginalis. A
Expedited partner treatment for patients with gonococcal or nongonococcal urethritis is recommended. B
Urethritis is defined by urethral inflammation and can result from infectious or non-infectious conditions.
Although characterized by purulent or mucoid discharge and dysuria, the condition may be asymptomatic.
Urethritis is a common presentation of sexually transmitted infection (STI) in young adult men. The annual incidence of STIs in the United States is estimated at 20 million new cases (2008)

Chlamydia is the most common cause of urethritis with 1.8 million reported cases in 2018. Twice as many cases were reported in females, likely reflecting wider screening in women and suggesting underdiagnosis in men.
Gonorrhea is the second most common cause with 580,000 reported cases in 2018. Gonorrhea rates have increased among men since 2014.
About half of the patients affected with STIs are 15 to 24 years old.

The overall prevalence of chlamydia is 6% to 7% among asymptomatic men in the United States. As many as 18% to 20% of men attending inner-city primary care clinics have chlamydia, and the prevalence is even greater in adolescent populations.
Compared with the general male population, there is higher prevalence of urethritis among men who have sex with men (MSM) (10% vs. 4%, P < .001) and in those with other STIs.
Individuals with STIs shoulder a tremendous physical, social, psychological, and economic burden, with an estimated lifetime cost of US$15.6 billion for STIs contracted in 2008.
In the United States, genitourinary symptoms comprise 4.4% of all ambulatory visits by adult men (over 18 years old).
See for common causes of urethritis.
Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the two most common causative organisms.
Coinfection is common, with multiple causative organisms found in 8.3% of patients in one study.
Approximately half of nongonococcal urethritis cases do not have an identified causative organism.

In a case-control study that excluded patients with GC organisms, Chlamydia trachomatis (20%), Mycoplasma genitalium (9%), adenoviruses (4%), and herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 (2%) were the most common causative agents.
Mycoplasma genitalium is a growing cause of urethritis, now accounting for 10-25% of nongonococcal cases in the United States.
Trichomonas vaginalis can cause urethritis in men who have sex with women, but is less common (1-8%) and prevalence varies substantially by location and patient populations.

Urethritis may be associated with other infectious conditions of the genitourinary tract including urinary tract infection, epididymitis, prostatitis, and orchitis. Approximately half of men with chronic nonbacterial prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome have urethral inflammation without any identifiable microorganisms.
Infectious organisms and noninfectious agents can produce inflammation of the urethra and the associated symptoms of urethritis.

Chronic urethritis, which is also called urethral syndrome, is an ill-defined symptom complex felt to be due to dysfunctional urinary epithelium and potassium recycling, as seen in persons with interstitial cystitis, chronic pelvic pain, and urethral syndrome.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Men who have sex with men

list.listitem: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends annual screening for chlamydia and gonorrhea in sexually active MSM at sites of sexual contact (i.e. urethra, rectum) and screening every 3 to 6 months in MSM at increased risk for STIs (i.e. on PrEP, HIV infection, multiple sexual partners). B
Current evidence is insufficient regarding screening for chlamydia or gonorrhea in men who have sex with women, but can be considered in high-risk populations. B
Primary prevention includes sex education, sexual behavior change, and routine condom use. A
Post-exposure prophylaxis with a single dose of doxycycline reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections including chlamydia and gonorrhea in high risk men who have sex with men.
Secondary prevention includes screening at-risk individuals, prompt treatment of infected individuals, sexual partner treatment, and test of cure when appropriate. B
Suspect urethritis in sexually active men who present with dysuria, urethral pruritus and/or penile discharge. C
If available, point-of-care testing (Gram stain of urethral secretions or first-void urine microscopic testing) can confirm the diagnosis. C
All men with suspected or confirmed urethritis should be tested for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis using urine NAAT-based testing. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pressure, and pain
Flank/back pain, fever, nausea, and dysuria
Testicular pain, dysuria, urge to urinate, painful intercourse and/or ejaculation, and scrotal swelling with warmth
Low back pain, perineal pain, fever, urinary retention, and pain with ejaculation

list.listitem: Urethritis should be suspected in all men with dysuria, urethral pruritus and/or penile discharge.

Symptoms may develop insidiously or acutely. Urgency and frequency may simulate UTI. Fever is rare. STIs in men typically present genitally with ulcerative lesions, adenopathy, urethritis, or some combination of these.
Infection can often be asymptomatic. Studies have found 10% of men with gonococcal infection, 25%-60% with chlamydial infection and 27% with Mycoplasma infection to be asymptomatic.

Ask patients about the duration, nature, quantity, quality (mucoid, serous, or purulent) of any discharge and/or dysuria. In 1 study, men with symptoms or an observable urethral discharge were more likely to have C. trachomatis detected (OR 6.9; 95% CI, 1.4-33.9) but not other nongonococcal urethritis organisms. In another study in France, all pathogens were more common in patients with discharge.

A detailed sexual history should include the number of partners, frequency of sexual activity, partner gender and their symptom status, presence of anal-receptive or anal-intermissive sex,sexual contact with sex workers or sex tourism.

Past medical history should include previous STIs, urethral discharge, epididymitis, urinary infections, prostatitis, pharmacotherapy for STIs, prior STI tests performed, and history of genitourinary or pelvic surgery or procedures. A detailed personal history should include drug abuse, sexual assault, and history of incarceration (associated with increased gonococcal urethritis).

Note associated symptoms including testicular pain, fever or chills, urinary urgency, frequency, hematuria, hematospermia, joint and musculoskeletal symptoms, back pain, skin lesions, joint swellings, rectal pain (anal sex), oral symptoms or lesions (oral exposure), and conjunctival symptoms.

Because urination may temporarily eliminate visible discharge and dilute material for Gram stain, at least 2 hours should pass without urination before taking a urethral specimen. Inspection of undergarments may disclose discharge or stain. Examination of the penis, scrotum, testes and epididymis, rectum, and prostate, coupled with palpation for regional lymph nodes, is appropriate. If foreskin is present, retraction will facilitate examination for periurethral inflammation or discharge and allow a more complete examination of the glans penis. Even in the absence of discharge, symptoms or high-risk exposure mandate acquisition of a urethral specimen (for culture, Gram stain, or PCR testing, and depending on the circumstance). Excessive meatitis (meatal inflammation) may be associated with a viral etiology.

Per the 2021 CDC guidelines, point-of-care testing (when available) demonstrating any of the following can confirm the diagnosis of urethritis: Presence of mucoid, mucopurulent or purulent discharge on examination. Gram stain of urethral secretions demonstrating ≥2 WBC per oil immersion field Positive leukocyte esterase or ≥10 WBC on microscopic examination of sediment from first-void urine.
Using a cutoff of ≥2 WBC/hpf, the estimated sensitivity of urethral Gram stain is 93% for C. trachomatis and approaching 100% for N. gonorrhoeae.
Gram stain may demonstrate intracellular gram negative or purple diplococci, diagnosing gonococcal urethritis.
Testing to identify C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae should be obtained in all men with suspected or confirmed urethritis.
Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is preferred for detection of C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae and urine is the preferred specimen in males based on 2021 CDC guidelines.

NAAT testing for M. genitalium and T. vaginalis are not recommended as part of the initial evaluation of urethritis, but urine testing should be considered (if available) in persistent or recurrent cases.
Follow patients with negative NAAT testing closely. If the results are positive, treat appropriately and refer sexual partners for evaluation and/or treatment.
Suspect urethritis in men with dysuria, penile discharge or urethral pruritus; genital ulcers or inguinal adenopathy are further indicative of an STI.
Consider Gram stain or first-void urine leukocyte esterase/microscopy (if available) to establish the diagnosis.
In all men with confirmed or suspected urethritis, obtain NAAT testing for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae.

Empiric therapy is recommended in symptomatic or laboratory confirmed cases of urethritis; if patient is asymptomatic and negative on testing of discharge or urine, treatment can await results of diagnostic testing.

Notify partners (if within the preceding 60 days) of patients with urethritis; expedited partner treatment (prescription given to patient for partners or treatment offered to partners without examination) is recommended by the CDC.
Chlamydia and gonorrhea are reportable infectious diseases. Providers should notify state and local public health authorities of all confirmed cases within 24 hours of diagnosis.
Providers should consider urethritis in transgender patients and adapt screening, diagnostic and treatment recommendations based on the patient’s current anatomy.
Treat gonococcal infection with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose. Treat chlamydia with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. A

An alternative regimen for gonococcal infection if ceftriaxone is not available or in the event of allergy is gentamicin 240 mg IM as a single dose plus azithromycin 2 grams orally as a single dose. A

If objective symptoms are recurrent or persistent, consider testing and treatment for M. genitalium and T. vaginalis. Treatment options for M. genitalium include doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, followed by moxifloxacin 400 mg orally once daily for 7 days. T. vaginalis should be treated with metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose or tinidazole 2 g orally in a single dose. A
Expedited partner treatment (partners within the preceding 60 days) for patients with gonococcal or nongonococcal urethritis is recommended. B
The CDC guidelines recommend treatment with antibiotics as soon as urethritis is diagnosed (see ).

When available, point-of-care gram stain of urethral discharge should be used to direct therapy based on the most likely organism: If gram-negative intracellular diplococi are identified, patients should be treated for presumed gonococcal infection. If no gram-negative intracellular diplocci are present, patient should be treated for nongonococcal urethritis. If point-of-care gram stain is not available, patients diagnosed with urethritis should be treated with a regimen efective against both gonorrhea and chlamydia.

Based on 2021 CDC guidelines, nongonococcal urethritis treatment options include:. First-line : Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Alternative option: Azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose (consider in patients who may not complete a multi-day drug regimen). In general azithromycin should be avoided due to rising resistance in C. trachomatis and M. genitalium.

Gonococcal infection options include: First-line: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose. For patients weighing more than 150 kg: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM in a single dose. Alternative option: Cefixime 800 mg orally in a single dose. Cephalosporin allergic patients: Gentamicin 240 mg IM in a single dose PLUS azithromycin 2 g orally in a single dose.
Unless chlamydia infection is excluded by NAAT testing, patients with gonococcal infection should be empirically treated for chlamydia.

In cases of persistent or recurrent nongonococcal urethritis, M. genitalium and T. vaginalis are common causes. If available, testing for these organisms should be performed. If testing is not available, patients should be empirically treated for these organisms based on risk factors and local prevalence data.

Treatment for M. genitalium urethritis should be directed by resistance data when available (the provider should presume macrolide resistance when data not available): If macrolide sensitive: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, followed by azithromycin 1 g orally once followed by 500 mg orally once daily for 3 additional days If macrolide resistant or no resistance data available: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, followed by moxifloxacin 400 mg orally once daily for 7 days

Men who have sex with women with recurrent or persistent nongonococcal urethritis should be tested and presumptively treated for T. vaginalis with metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose or tinidazole 2 g orally in a single dose. The patient’s partners should also be referred for evaluation and treatment.

Treat patients who have recurrent symptoms with antibiotics only when there is objective evidence of recurrent urethritis. If the patient did not comply with the initial treatment or was re-exposed by the same inadequately treated partner, a repeated course of the initial therapy is appropriate for both.

Uncommonly, persons who feel they may have been exposed to an STI may wish to have empiric treatment. Although confirmation of STI status is always preferred in the asymptomatic patient, it is reasonable to offer treatment that is curative for both gonococcal and chlamydial infection on a contact basis. Similarly, patients at high risk for infection who are unlikely to return for a follow-up evaluation merit consideration for empiric therapy for GC and chlamydia. Whenever possible, evaluate and treat partners of patients treated empirically.

All sexual partners of men with urethritis within the preceding 60 days should be evaluated and treated. Expedited partner treatment (prescription given to patient for their partners or treatment offered to partners without examination) is recommended by the CDC. In 1 study, expedited treatment reduced the risk of recurrent infection in the original patient, especially for a patient with gonorrhea (3% vs. 11%; NNT = 12.5).Readers are advised to familiarize themselves with local governance concerning whether or not partners may be treated on an epidemiologic basis, without direct examination.

Persistent symptoms in the absence of urologic pathology or infection supports a provisional diagnosis of chronic nonbacterial prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome or urethral syndrome, for which some clinicians advise a clinical trial of metronidazole 2 g orally as a single dose.
Provide STI education and counseling as needed.

Patients with recurrent or persistent urethritis despite appropriate initial therapy and empiric treatment for M. genitalium and T. vaginalis should be referred to a urologist or infectious disease expert.

Urethritis is generally treated in the outpatient setting. Hospitalization may be required in disseminated gonococcal disease or urethritis in the setting of a severe inflammatory disorder like Stevens-Johnson syndrome or in some cases of Reiter's syndrome.

Men with urethritis may also have other urogenital infections including cystitis, pyelonephritis, epididymitis, orchitis, and prostatitis. Include consideration of these comorbidities in the initial urethritis evaluation.
Urethral stricture may be a consequence of urethritis, especially gonococcal. When stricture is present, urology referral is warranted.

Gonococcal urethritis may be complicated by disseminated gonorrhea, with fever, skin lesions, arthralgias, and tenosynovitis; perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome) is an uncommon consequence of gonococcal infection at any body site (except pelvic gonococcal infections in women).
Another consequence of urethritis is infertility. There is a strong association with infertility and presence of chlamydial antibodies in the serum and semen.
Gonococcal and chlamydial infections can infect the conjunctiva. Oculogenital syndrome (conjunctivitis accompanied by urethritis) is commonly caused by Chlamydia.

Postgonococcal urethritis (PGU) is a common complication of gonococcal urethritis. PGU is suspected when the urethral smear shows the presence of polymorphonuclear leukocytes 7 to 14 days after gonococcal infection treatment. It is often associated with chlamydial coinfection. Less frequently, M. genitalium, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma parvum biovar 1, and U. urealyticum biovar 2 are comorbid with gonococcal urethritis. The presence of concomitant M. genitalium organisms greatly increases the risk of PGU (up to 14-fold), but treatment regimens that are effective for both pathogens reduce this likelihood.

Reiter's syndrome (reactive arthritis) is a group of inflammatory conditions involving the joints, urethra, and eyes. There may also be lesions on the skin and mucous membranes. This is commonly associated with C. trachomatis and typically presents after 1 to 3 weeks of the infection.
Most patients do well with initial therapy for dual infections (gonococcal and chlamydial), and treatment failures generally respond well after a second treatment. C
Persistence of pain, discomfort, and irritative voiding symptoms beyond 3 months should alert the clinician to the possibility of chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome. A
A few patients develop systemic infection requiring hospitalization and IV antibiotics. Other patients may develop reactive arthritis and run a chronic course with other systemic symptoms. C
Test for other STIs, including syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis, in persons who are diagnosed with a new STI. B

Most patients do well with initial therapy for dual infections (gonococcal and chlamydial), and treatment failures generally respond well to a second treatment. Teenagers may be particularly prone to high recurrence rates, but this is likely due to poor compliance and high rates of reinfection.
Persistence of pain, discomfort, and irritative voiding symptoms beyond 3 months should alert the clinician to the possibility of chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men.
A few patients develop systemic infection requiring hospitalization and IV antibiotics. Other patients may develop reactive arthritis and run a chronic course with other systemic symptoms.

Test of cure is not recommended when patients are asymptomatic following appropriate antibiotic treatment. However, testing for reinfection is now recommended 3 months following treatment, regardless of whether sexual partners have been treated.

Persistence/recurrence of symptoms should prompt careful laboratory retesting. The fact that symptoms persist after effective treatment is not rare: as many as 36% of men who had been successfully treated (test-of-cure organism negative) manifested urethritis symptoms 3 to 4 weeks posttreatment (PGU). Symptoms alone, without laboratory evidence of urethral inflammation, are insufficient to institute retreatment.
Test for other STIs, including syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis, in persons who are diagnosed with a new STI.
In cases of persistent or recurrent symptoms, M. genitalium and T. vaginalis NAAT testing (intraurethral swab or first-void urine) is recommended (if available).
For recurrent or persistent urethritis, perform a comprehensive urologic examination if one has not yet been done.
Instruct patients to abstain from sexual intercourse for at least 7 days after therapy is initiated, and until their symptoms have resolved and their sex partners have been adequately treated.
Most cases of urethritis are related to an STI. Prevention and control of STIs should reduce or prevent urethritis. Minimizing sexual partners, condom use, and abstinence are ways to prevent STI.
If symptoms persist, adequate follow-up tests and abstinence from sex during the therapy period are necessary.
Sexual partners of the preceding 60 days need to be treated.
Patients should avoid high-risk sexual behavior and limit their number of partners. Proper use of a condom for every sexual act is advised to minimize the STIs.

Because the proportion of older men who have an underlying STI as the cause of urethritis is substantially less than in younger men, a negative screen for STIs should prompt searching for other causes.

Repeat infection is much more common among teens and young adults. Test of cure, adequate follow up, and education on routine use of condoms and advice to reduce in high-risk sexual behavior should occur.

Urethritis in prepubertal boys is most often caused by trauma, local irritants or viruses. The presence of discharge or laboratory findings suggestive of infectious etiologies such as gonorrhea or chlamydia should prompt evaluation for sexual abuse.

feature.feature_body:
Cause Organism, Chemical, or Condition
Bacteria
Chlamydia trachomatis (25%)
Neisseria gonorrhoeae (21%)
Mycoplasma genitalium (8%)
Ureaplasma urealyticum (5%)
Coliform bacteria
Haemophilus vaginalis
Treponema pallidum
Protozoaa
Trichomonas vaginalis (3%)
Viruses Herpes simplex virus, adenoviruses, human papillomavirus (HPV)
Fungi
Candida albicans
Chemicals Chemical irritation of the urethra (eg, condom, bath products)
Traumab Urinary procedures, accidents, instrumentations, foreign bodies, catheterizations (more common with intermittent and long-term catheter use), some chemical irritants (eg, spermicides, certain bath products), and high-intensity sexual activity
Inflammatory conditions Generalized illness, eg, reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome), Wegener's granulomatosis, Behcet's disease, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Tumor
Uncommon organisms associated with oral sex
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus parainfluenzae, adenoviruses, and herpes simplex virus 1
